content: Management of lymphatic filariasis-related conditions involves several key components. These include maintaining proper hygiene, ensuring meticulous care of the skin and wounds, and implementing elevation and exercise regimens to enhance lymphatic circulation. Additionally, healthcare facilities must be equipped to provide antibiotic therapy and symptomatic management for acute attacks of adenolymphangitis (ADL). If surgical services are unavailable at the district or implementation unit (IU) level, it is acknowledged that not all districts or IUs can provide such services. However, at least one surgical facility should be designated to serve all IUs with patients, such as a regional hospital. In districts with fewer patients, the minimum package of care must still be accessible. The ultimate goal is to achieve 100% geographic coverage for all known patients. It is important to recognize that patient estimates may underestimate the true number of cases due to the long latency period of lymphoedema and hydrocele, and new cases may emerge over time. Services provided by non-governmental organizations (NGOs) or private facilities can be considered designated facilities for the clinical care of lymphoedema or hydrocele. NGOs and private institutions play a significant role in morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) services. However, to ensure sustainability, the capacity of public facilities should also be strengthened. For national programs without a budget for MMDP, the national lymphatic filariasis (LF) elimination program is not expected to directly implement hydrocele surgeries or lymphoedema management. These services should be integrated into the healthcare system. However, the national LF elimination program is responsible for coordinating, monitoring, and evaluating these services, which will require resources. Specific activities led by national LF elimination programs include conducting situation analyses (including patient estimation), coordinating capacity strengthening, monitoring and reporting the availability of MMDP, and assessing readiness and quality. These activities can be integrated with other initiatives to optimize the use of limited resources. As countries scale down mass drug administration (MDA) activities, some funds may become available for MMDP. Additionally, LF morbidity management should remain a priority for inclusion in essential services under Universal Health Coverage and within the Sustainable Development Goals. To assist countries in implementing MMDP, a toolkit containing various resources has been prepared. This toolkit is accessible online and provides guidance for managing morbidity and preventing disability. Post-validation activities and surveillance are essential even after validation of LF elimination. These activities include ongoing surveillance for LF infection and ensuring care for lymphoedema and hydrocele patients. Post-validation activities should be integrated into existing health services to ensure sustainability. Integrated vector management should prioritize LF-endemic areas and align with efforts to control vectors of other diseases. Existing surveillance activities post-MDA can serve as the foundation for post-validation surveillance. WHO recommends tailoring surveillance activities to the specific context of each country, utilizing existing platforms for surveillance. These activities may include periodic cross-sectional surveys, routine surveillance of target population groups, and xenomonitoring. Programs must respond to surveillance results, which may involve testing and treatment, additional investigations to identify areas or groups for targeted treatment, and treating infected individuals according to national policy. The combined regimen of albendazole (400 mg) plus diethylcarbamazine (DEC, 6 mg/kg) or ivermectin (150–200 µg/kg), currently recommended for MDA, is also recommended for treating infected individuals. Treatment strategies should be directly observed. Post-validation surveillance results should be reported to WHO using the appropriate tools, such as the joint application package. Results should also be shared in meetings of Regional Program Managers and Regional Program Review Groups to facilitate discussions, identify challenges, and inform best practices in post-validation activities. WHO continues to monitor operational research to identify new diagnostic tools and standardized methods for post-validation surveillance to ensure infection levels remain below elimination thresholds and confirm the elimination of transmission.
